milestones.title: 2D Ising verification
milestones.result: peak at T=2.30 ± 0.05, Onsager: 2.2692
milestones.question_plain: If you heat a sheet of tiny magnets, is there an exact temperature where they suddenly stop agreeing with each other?
milestones.why_it_matters: It is the simplest place in physics where a whole system flips from order to chaos at one sharp tipping point, and it tests whether the lab's instrument can find that point at all.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — the lab found the tipping point at a temperature of about 2.30, right on top of the exact textbook answer of 2.2692.

milestones.title: Finite-size scaling
milestones.result: χ_max ∝ L^1.816 over L=32–256, R²=0.998; uses the |m|-susceptibility on the disordered side. L≥512 awaits a cluster updater — Metropolis critical slowing, see BACKLOG
milestones.question_plain: When you make the grid of magnets bigger and bigger, does the way it behaves near the tipping point follow one clean, predictable rule?
milestones.why_it_matters: If the same hidden pattern shows up at every size, it means the behavior at the tipping point is universal, not an accident of one particular grid.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — across grids from 32 up to 256 on a side, the sharpness of the change grew in lockstep with grid size as a clean power law, close to the exact textbook prediction.

milestones.title: Critical exponent β from data collapse of M·L^(β/ν) vs (T-T_c)·L^(1/ν)
milestones.result: β/ν = 0.131 over L=16–48 via Wolff cluster updates, residual 8.2e-3 vs exact 1/8; rescaled magnetization curves collapse onto one master curve. A short proof run gave 0.122; both bracket 1/8.
milestones.question_plain: As the magnets approach the tipping point, exactly how fast does their shared order melt away?
milestones.why_it_matters: The precise speed at which order disappears is a fingerprint shared by many different materials, so measuring it confirms the lab is reading the deep, universal physics.
milestones.result_plain: The lab measured that fading-rate fingerprint and landed right on the exact textbook value of one-eighth, with all the size curves folding neatly onto a single shared curve.

milestones.title: Specific heat curve C(T)
milestones.result: C-peak at T=2.275 vs Onsager exact 2.2692, rel. err 0.2%; χ-peak cross-check 2.280 from the same run, L=128, 25 temps in [2.0, 2.6], 40k sweeps, 33s on GPU. A second, thermal calibration of the same T_c the magnetization found in M01. The finite-L peak sits just above the infinite-volume value, as expected; the exact log amplitude A=(2/π)(2/T_c)²≈0.495 isn't resolved by a finite lattice, so the calibrated claim is the peak location, not the amplitude.
milestones.question_plain: Right at the tipping point, does the sheet of magnets suddenly drink up an enormous gulp of heat?
milestones.why_it_matters: Measuring the heat-hungry spike is a completely separate way to pinpoint the tipping temperature, so agreeing with the magnetism measurement proves the lab isn't fooling itself.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — the heat-hunger spiked at a temperature of about 2.275, matching the exact textbook tipping point of 2.2692 to within a fraction of a percent and confirming the answer the magnetism gave earlier.

milestones.title: Verify lattice geometries beyond square
milestones.result: triangular verified: χ-peak T_c(L=129) = 3.675 vs exact 4/ln3 = 3.6410, rel. err 0.9%; specific-heat peak independently at T_c = 3.650 from the same run, 25 temps in [3.3, 4.0], 40k sweeps, 63s on GPU. The triangular lattice is non-bipartite, so the square red/black checkerboard is physically wrong here — this needed a 3-sublattice update with color(i,j)=(i+2j)%3, which only wraps cleanly when 3|L, hence L=129. Same 2D Ising universality class as M01, a different exact T_c — a clean geometry check. The finite-L peak sits just above the infinite-volume value, as expected. Hexagonal closed 2026-08-11 — M05 is now complete on both geometries: honeycomb χ-peak T_c(L=128) = 1.532 vs exact 2/ln(2+√3) = 1.5187, rel. err 0.9%; specific-heat peak independently at T_c = 1.526 from the same run, 25 temps in [1.35, 1.70], 40k sweeps, 33s on GPU, seed 42. The honeycomb is the triangular lattice's dual and its opposite in difficulty: with girth 6 it is bipartite, so it needs no 3-colouring at all — `ising.py`'s plain red/black checkerboard is already exact, and the awkward 3|L constraint becomes a mere even-L one (hence L=128, the square engine's own default). The lattice is brick-walled onto a square array: two horizontal neighbours plus one parity-selected vertical partner, (i+1,j) when (i+j) is even else (i−1,j). That parity rule is the entire physics delta and the entire risk surface, so it is locked by exact small-lattice tests rather than by the thermal run — degree exactly 3, adjacency symmetric, bipartite under (i+j)%2, girth ≥ 6 (no 4-cycles, which is what separates it from a square lattice), 3N/2 bonds, ground state exactly −1.5 per spin, and the vectorised neighbour sum reproduced bond-for-bond against an independently loop-written reference. Three lattices now carry three exact T_c ordered exactly as coordination number demands: z=3 → 1.5187, z=4 → 2.2692, z=6 → 3.6410. The run that failed first, and what it bought: the initial canonical sweep (random start, the same 8k burn-in the triangular run used) reported T_c = 1.379, 9.2% low — not a geometry bug but a single L=128 lattice frozen in a system-spanning stripe domain at T=1.3792, ⟨|m|⟩=0.573 between neighbours of 0.913 and 0.895, a 46σ rise with temperature, χ=1164 against neighbours below 1.3. The bare argmax crowned it. This is the identical shape to M01's 2026-07-23 campaign pass 6, and it exposed a real gap: `check_m01` had carried a non-equilibration guard since that incident and `check_m05` had not. Two fixes landed — the engine defaults to an ordered start (with only three bonds per site a domain wall is cheaper and dissolves more slowly than on the square or triangular lattices, and clearing a wrapping wall costs O(L²) sweeps), and `check_m05` now applies the same `nonequilibrated_indices` guard, disclosing any exclusion by temperature rather than dropping it quietly. The failed run's arrays are kept verbatim as the regression fixture in `tests/test_checks.py`; the guard alone recovers T_c = 1.537 from that very data. Grade: rung-0 verification — the instrument checking itself against an Onsager-class exact result on a lattice it had not touched. A completion of M05's documented open edge, explicitly not a discovery. Same single-L finite-size caveat as the triangular half: the pseudo-critical peak sits just above the infinite-volume value, and an L-extrapolation would sharpen it.
milestones.question_plain: If you rearrange the same tiny magnets onto a differently shaped grid, does the tipping point move to a new temperature but still follow the same deep rules?
milestones.why_it_matters: Showing that the shape of the grid changes the exact tipping temperature yet not the underlying behavior is a clean demonstration of one of physics' most beautiful ideas: that wildly different systems can obey the very same deep rules.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — twice over. On a triangular grid, where each magnet touches six others, the lab found the tipping point at about 3.675, close to its own exact answer of 3.641. On a honeycomb grid, where each magnet touches only three, it found about 1.532 against an exact 1.519. Both are far from the square grid's 2.269, and they line up in exactly the order you'd guess: the fewer neighbors holding a magnet in line, the less heat it takes to break the order. Three shapes, three different tipping points, same deep behavior underneath.

milestones.title: 3D simple cubic Ising
milestones.result: χ-peak T_c(L=12) = 4.504 vs MC benchmark 4.5115, rel. err 0.17%; specific-heat peak independently at T_c ≈ 4.42. CPU NumPy engine, 21 temps in [4.1, 4.9], 16k sweeps, 28s. Single-L Metropolis estimate — the small-L pseudo-critical peak carries an O(L^−1/ν) finite-size shift, so this is a calibration pass, not a precision T_c; an L-extrapolation would sharpen it. See BACKLOG.
milestones.question_plain: If we stack the tiny magnets into a solid block instead of a flat sheet, does it still freeze into order, and at what temperature?
milestones.why_it_matters: Real magnets are three-dimensional, so this checks the lab against the world we actually live in, where adding a dimension changes everything.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — the block of tiny magnets locked into order right where the known answer says it should, near a temperature of about 4.5.

milestones.title: Potts model (q-state)
milestones.result: all four exact T_c = 1/ln(1+√q) reproduced from the order-parameter χ peak on an L=64 square lattice, 25 temps per q in T_c±0.12, Wolff cluster updates: q=3 → 1.002 vs 0.995 (0.7%), q=4 → 0.907 vs 0.910 (0.3%), q=5 → 0.822 vs 0.852 (3.5%), q=6 → 0.749 vs 0.808 (7.2%); 471s on GPU. The continuous→first-order change is clear in the susceptibility curves: peak χ_max climbs monotonically 134 → 370 (continuous q≤4) → 824 → 1063 (first-order q≥5) — the taller, sharper spike of a discontinuous transition. Single-spin Metropolis is metastably trapped through this transition and reports noisy multi-peaked χ (a first attempt did exactly that); the Wolff single-cluster updater — Potts FK bond prob p=1−exp(−βJ), recolour the cluster to a random new flavour — fixes it, reusing wolff.py's cluster mechanics. q=5,6 are first-order with stronger finite-size/metastability shifts, so they carry a wider ±0.15 tolerance (vs ±0.1 for the continuous q≤4) — a physical allowance, not a fudge; both still land well inside it. The order parameter is the Potts m=(q·ρ_max−1)/(q−1).
milestones.question_plain: If each tiny magnet can point in more than two directions, is there a tipping point where the way it freezes changes from gentle to sudden?
milestones.why_it_matters: It shows that a small change in the rules — how many choices each magnet has — can flip a smooth gradual change into an abrupt all-at-once one.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — with up to four choices the freezing came on gradually, but with five or more it snapped on all at once, and the lab pinpointed each transition temperature along the way.

milestones.title: 2D XY model
milestones.result: helicity-modulus jump crossing T_BKT(L=64) = 0.913 vs benchmark 0.8929, rel. err 2.2%; the spin stiffness Υ(T) crosses the Nelson-Kosterlitz universal-jump line Υ=(2/π)T at the transition, located by linear interpolation of the first downward root of Υ(T)−(2/π)T, 26 temps in [0.6, 1.1], 40k sweeps, 94s on GPU. This is the first model with continuous spins — angles θ∈[0,2π
milestones.question_plain: Can a flat sheet of magnets that can spin in any direction still have a special temperature, even when it never truly freezes into a single direction?
milestones.why_it_matters: It reveals a subtler kind of order, built from tiny whirlpools rather than everything pointing the same way, that won a Nobel Prize.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — even though the sheet never settles into one direction, the lab found the special temperature where its stiffness suddenly gives way, close to the known value of about 0.89.

milestones.title: 2D Heisenberg (continuous spins)
milestones.result: the absence of order reproduced: at a fixed T=0.7 the per-spin vector magnetization ⟨|m|⟩ drifts 0.478 → 0.282 → 0.142 across L=16, 32, 64 (each step ×0.59, ×0.50 < 1; slope vs 1/L = +7.05 > 0, so ⟨|m|⟩ → 0 as L → ∞), 20k sweeps/L, 250s on GPU. This is the rare milestone whose correct answer is a NEGATIVE one — Mermin-Wagner forbids a 2D system with a continuous (here O(3)) symmetry from spontaneously ordering at any T > 0, and unlike the XY model (M08) the Heisenberg sphere S² is simply connected (π₁=0, no stable vortices), so there is no BKT escape either — no transition of any kind at finite T. The falsifiable signature is the finite-size drift of ⟨|m|⟩ toward 0; reading a single small L instead would fake an appreciable ⟨|m|⟩ and a spurious transition (the #1 way this ships wrong), so the run varies L and check_m09 asserts the monotone decrease + positive 1/L slope. The energy per spin is L-independent (≈ -1.15 at every size — an intensive quantity), the receipt that it's the order parameter washing out, not the lattices sitting at different states. New O(3) engine (heisenberg.py): 3-component unit-vector spins, E = −J·Σ S_i·S_j, uniform-on-sphere sampling (z=cosθ ∈ [−1,1] uniform, φ ∈ [0,2π) — NOT θ-uniform, which pole-biases and corrupts every energy/correlation
milestones.question_plain: If the tiny magnets can point anywhere in three-dimensional space but live on a flat sheet, can they ever all line up?
milestones.why_it_matters: The honest, surprising answer — no, never — is one of the deepest rules in physics, and confirming an absence is harder than finding a signal.
milestones.result_plain: No, and that is the correct answer: as the sheet was made larger the magnetism faded steadily toward nothing, exactly as the famous no-ordering rule predicts.

milestones.title: Antiferromagnetic Ising on a bipartite lattice (same as ferromagnetic by sign-flip — sanity check the framework handles negative J cleanly)
milestones.result: staggered χ_s-peak T_N(L=128) = 2.282 vs Onsager exact 2.2692, rel. err 0.5%; specific-heat peak independently at 2.276 from the same run, 25 temps in [2.0, 2.6], 40k sweeps, 30s on GPU. J=−1 (antiferromagnetic) on the square lattice: by the bipartite sublattice gauge flip s_i→−s_i (on one colour) the AFM is exactly the ferromagnet in disguise, so the Néel point is Onsager's same T_c — the framework handles negative coupling cleanly. The order parameter is the staggered magnetization m_s = (1/N)Σ ε_i s_i with ε=(−1)^(x+y); its susceptibility χ_s peaks at T_N. The headline trap: the uniform ⟨|m|⟩ stays ≈0 at all T (≤0.003 across the whole sweep — the Néel state carries no net moment), so reading uniform m would show nothing and look broken. The square lattice is bipartite and unfrustrated, so the plain red/black checkerboard is exact — NO 3-colouring (that was M05's frustrated triangular problem; the frustrated triangular AFM is the later M13). Strongest correctness guard: an AFM↔FM gauge-duality cross-check test — the AFM's staggered observables equal an FM run's uniform observables bond-for-bond at the same |J|/seed (catches a silent ΔE sign-error that would secretly revert to the FM). The only code change from ising.py is the sign of J in ΔE; ising.py is untouched and its _neighbor_sum reused. The finite-L peak sits just above the infinite-volume value, as expected — the same finite-L peak caveat as M04 applies.
milestones.question_plain: If we flip the rule so neighboring magnets want to point opposite ways instead of the same way, does the lab still handle it cleanly?
milestones.why_it_matters: Many real materials are built from opposites pulling against each other, so this proves the lab can handle that mirror-image world too.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — the alternating up-down pattern froze in at the same temperature its same-direction cousin does, confirming the lab handles the flipped rule correctly.

milestones.title: Edwards-Anderson spin glass on a 2D square lattice
milestones.result: The finite-T transition — T_SG ≈ 1.10 for ±J couplings, with a Binder-cumulant crossing — is the 3D case — that's M12, not this. The original "develops structure at low T" phrasing was corrected to the T_c = 0 framing in the M11 PR.
milestones.question_plain: If you tangle a magnet so its tiny parts pull in random, conflicting directions, can it ever freeze into a locked pattern at a real, above-zero temperature?
milestones.why_it_matters: It tells us whether messy, frustrated materials behave like ordinary magnets or live by stranger rules, and it shows the lab can honestly report a 'no' as proudly as a 'yes'.
milestones.result_plain: In flat, two-dimensional form it never truly freezes at any real temperature: the disorder keeps spreading wider and wider as the lab cools toward absolute zero, with no single moment of locking-in.

milestones.title: 3D EA spin glass — the harder, more famous case
milestones.result: code merged 2026-07-01, PR #43 — the quick-CPU calibration ships a [~] null: at L=4,6,8 × 8 disorder realizations the multi-L Binder crossing resolves to T_SG≈0.56, so the finite-T crossing does not resolve at CPU scale — report reports/2026-07-04-m12.html. The GPU promotion run happened 2026-07-22 — L=6,8,10 × 200 realizations with parallel tempering, receipt reports/receipts/run-2026-07-22-m12.json — and returned a second null: crossing_T = 1.244 against the 0.95±0.15 band configured at the time. The 2026-08-01 audit found two defects that invalidate that run as a promotion gate. First, the PT swap scheduler derived swap parity from the sweep index, so the production default swap_every=10 pinned parity to 0 and odd-gap replica pairs were never attempted — the ladder decomposed into isolated 2-rung pairs, visible in the receipt as exactly 0.0 at every odd gap of swap_rate_by_L; PR #68 fixes this by counting swap rounds. Second, the 0.95 benchmark was the Gaussian-disorder value graded against a bimodal ±J simulation, so even a converged run near the correct ≈1.102 could not have passed; PR #68 corrects the benchmark and tolerance, with the checks.py mirror updated in its stacked follow-up. The 2026-07-01/04 CPU nulls ran swap_every=5 [odd] and are unaffected by the parity defect. Promotion to [x] now requires: [1] the parity fix and corrected benchmark merged, [2] a fresh multi-L GPU run whose crossing lands within the corrected tolerance, [3] human review of that run. [1] and [2] are now MET; [3] is open, which is why this is [?] and not [x]. The 2026-08-24 hero run — L=6,8,10,12 on one 0.80-1.60 ladder of 16 rungs, 800 disorder realizations x 2 replicas, 100k burn-in + 100k measurement sweeps per size, 4.4 GPU-hours — lands the Binder crossing at T_SG = 1.124 against the 1.102 benchmark (tol 0.10), with the equilibration guard at max|<q>| = 0.001 and PT health `ok` at all four sizes (swap 0.48-0.81). `check_m12` re-derives it: True. The honest uncertainty is larger than that number looks. The six pairwise crossings scatter 0.973-1.184 (mean 1.074, sem 0.031 -> 0.9 sigma from the literature 1.1019(29)), and five of the six would pass the tolerance individually while 8x10 alone would fail low at 0.973 — so the verdict is pair-selection-dependent, and the defensible claim is consistent with T_SG ~ 1.10 at +/-0.1, not a measurement of 1.124. A second estimator now rides along: xi_L/L, the second-moment correlation length of the overlap field, whose crossing is 1.229 (pairwise mean 1.150, 1.7 sigma high). The two estimators bracket the literature value (1.074 < 1.1019 < 1.150). A mid-flight hypothesis that the Binder cumulant was biased HIGH relative to xi/L — from a short 6k-sweep L=6/10 probe reading 1.288 vs 1.199 — did not survive the full run, which inverts the order; that probe was noise-dominated and is recorded here so nobody re-derives it. Receipt `reports/receipts/run-2026-08-24-0324-m12.json`; rerun `lab m12 --L-values 6,8,10,12 --t-min 0.80 --t-max 1.60 --realizations 800 --sweeps 100000 --burnin 100000 --swap-every 5 --seed 20260823`.
milestones.question_plain: Give that same tangled, conflicting magnet a third dimension to live in — does the extra room finally let it freeze into a glassy, locked-up state at a real temperature?
milestones.why_it_matters: This is the famous case behind real glassy materials, and finding the freezing point would prove the lab can reach the genuinely hard problems, not just the textbook ones.
milestones.result_plain: Not yet — and both times the reason was found here, in the lab's own setup. The first attempt was too small to see anything. The second looked like a real answer until an audit turned up two faults: the simulation runs copies of the material at a ladder of temperatures and trades neighbours between rungs, and one whole set of those pairs was never tried even once, so the ladder broke into isolated couples instead of one connected chain; and the textbook number it was being graded against had been measured for a different kind of randomness than the one being simulated. Both faults are fixed in the code; the experiment is owed a rerun. Until then this stays grey.

milestones.title: Triangular lattice antiferromagnet — frustrated, ordered ground states are degenerate
milestones.result: residual entropy reproduced: S0/N = 0.3338 k_B vs Wannier 0.3383, Δ=0.0045, by thermodynamic integration S0 = ln2 − ∫ C dlnT = ln2 − ∫(C/T)dT on the frustrated J=−1 triangular antiferromagnet, L=24, 40 geometric temps in 0.15–12.0; ground-state energy exact −1.0000/spin; check_m13 re-integrates C/T within its own ±0.03 tolerance — report reports/2026-07-04-m13.html, PR #44.
milestones.question_plain: When you arrange tiny magnets on triangles so they can never all satisfy each other, the material has many equally-good resting states — how much built-in disorder does that leave behind?
milestones.why_it_matters: Counting that leftover freedom reveals how nature copes when there is no single 'happy' arrangement, a puzzle at the heart of many exotic materials.
milestones.result_plain: The lab measured that leftover freedom by slowly warming the material from near absolute zero and adding up the heat it soaks in, and landed at about 0.334 — right on top of the exact textbook value of 0.338 for how much disorder frustrated triangles keep even at the coldest possible temperature.

milestones.title: Random-bond Ising (binary disorder p% antiferromagnetic bonds)
milestones.result: the exact Nishimori-line internal energy reproduced: the disorder-averaged energy per spin matches the exact identity E/N = −2·tanh(1/T) = −2(1−2p) across p ∈ [0.04, 0.16] on the Nishimori line (tanh(1/T)=1−2p) to max Δ = 0.015 (L=24, 64 ±J realizations, single-spin checkerboard Metropolis reusing M11's ±J bond machinery), 204s on CPU. This is a gauge-symmetry identity that holds at any lattice size — not a finite-size-shifted T_c — so it verifies cheaply and robustly; check_m14 re-derives −2·tanh(1/T) from each point's own T and re-grades the measured energy, a receipt not an echo. The multicritical Nishimori point itself (literature benchmark p_c ≈ 0.1094, T_c ≈ 0.9528) is mapped only APPROXIMATELY at this scale: the ferromagnetic ⟨|m|⟩ collapses 0.85 → 0.22 as p rises along the line, passing through ½ near p ≈ 0.126 and bracketing the benchmark, but the two-size (L=12,24) Binder-cumulant crossing does NOT resolve at reachable disorder averaging (the curves carry a large finite-size drift and do not cross in-window) — precise pinning of p_c is deferred to a large-L hero run. The green leaf is earned by the exact energy; the precise MNP stays a documented open edge. Report reports/2026-07-05-m14.html, PR — the lab's first result on a quenched-disorder phase diagram, and the first swept along an exactly-solvable line.
milestones.question_plain: If you sprinkle a magnet with a chosen fraction of contrary bonds that want their neighbours to disagree, is there a special recipe where order and disorder meet at a single magic point?
milestones.why_it_matters: That meeting point is a rare crossroads where several kinds of behaviour collide, and mapping it teaches how a pinch of randomness reshapes a whole material.
milestones.result_plain: Along a special, exactly-solvable path through the recipe book, the lab reproduced the known energy of this mixed magnet perfectly across every blend it tried. The magic point where order gives way to disorder shows up in roughly the right place, but pinning it down exactly needs a much bigger run — so that piece is left honestly open.

milestones.title: Glauber dynamics relaxation
milestones.result: machine check passed; reviewed 2026-08-02 — Ben's delegated batch approval, substance reviewed by Claude — the lab's first NON-equilibrium milestone. Measured coarsening exponent n = 0.486 ± 0.001 (stat), R² = 0.9999 from the correlation-length estimator (half-height of the equal-time G(r,t), computed by FFT/Wiener-Khinchin), with an independent energy-length cross-check L_e ∝ 1/(E−E_eq) giving n = 0.469; L=512, 48 random-quench seeds, single-spin Glauber / heat-bath dynamics [P(s→+1)=σ(2βh)], t up to 8000 sweeps quenched to T=1.498 ≈ 0.66·T_c, 34s on GPU. The domain length traces a clean power law over ~2.6 decades in t (L_c grows 4 → 73), and the effective exponent drifts UP to 0.494 on the late window — the textbook preasymptotic approach to the asymptotic Allen-Cahn ½. The measured exponent sits a few percent BELOW ½ — the well-documented finite-time correction (2D Ising coarsening approaches t^(1/2) from below). The defensible statement is n ≈ 0.47–0.49 with a systematic band of ±0.02 dominated by estimator/window choice — the ±0.001 OLS statistical error is misleadingly tiny (it only reflects how straight the log-log line is) and is deliberately NOT quoted as the uncertainty. #1 failure mode: reaching for a cluster (Wolff) updater — it flips whole domains at once and destroys the very coarsening being measured; M15 uses single-spin heat-bath only, and the x-axis IS real Monte-Carlo time. Second guard: a seed frozen into a metastable stripe (rare at 0.66·T_c) would saturate its L(t) — mitigated by averaging 48 seeds and excluding the finite-size-saturation tail from the fit window. `check_m15` re-selects the scaling window and re-fits the exponent from the saved L(t) (a receipt, not an echo). Report reports/2026-07-07-m15.html, PR.
milestones.question_plain: Cool a hot, scrambled magnet in an instant and watch patches of agreement start to spread — how fast do those patches grow as time ticks on?
milestones.why_it_matters: The same coarsening rhythm governs everything from cooling alloys to separating oil and water, so measuring its pace connects a toy magnet to the everyday physics of things settling down.
milestones.result_plain: The patches grew with a measured power of 0.47 to 0.49, against the predicted one-half. The spread is the real uncertainty: the growth law is approached from below, so a young pattern reads slightly low, and the number drifts up to 0.494 late in the run. Measured across 48 separate quenches on a 512-wide grid.

milestones.title: Aging in spin glasses
milestones.result: machine check passed; reviewed 2026-08-02 — Ben's delegated batch approval, substance reviewed by Claude. A 3D ±J Edwards–Anderson glass was quenched from T=∞ to T=0.60 and evolved with local single-spin Metropolis dynamics on L=12 across 64 independent disorder realizations. The saved C(t_w+Δt,t_w) table spans t_w=16,32,64,128 and Δt=8…256. Regrading the table gives a within-group RMS scatter for the aging variable Δt/t_w only 0.24× the time-translation-invariant Δt scatter (5 shared ratio groups vs 6 shared lag groups); independently, at fixed Δt=64 the correlation rises 0.714→0.818 as t_w grows, ΔC=+0.104, so the older glass decorrelates more slowly. This is the expected breaking of time-translation invariance. Boundary: finite L/time and one low temperature establish an aging calibration, not a universal scaling function; cluster updates and parallel-tempering swaps were deliberately forbidden because they would corrupt the physical clock. `check_m16` re-derives both collapse residuals and the fixed-lag separation from the saved table.
milestones.question_plain: After a tangled magnet is suddenly chilled, does it keep changing in a way that depends on how long ago it was chilled — in other words, does it carry a memory of its own age?
milestones.why_it_matters: This 'getting older' behaviour is how real glasses and disordered solids quietly evolve for years, and catching it would show the lab can study things that never fully settle.
milestones.result_plain: The older the magnet, the more strongly it held onto its past. Compared at a fixed delay, correlation with its own history rose from 0.714 to 0.818 as the magnet aged. Its four separate histories line up when time is measured relative to age rather than absolutely — scattering only a quarter as much that way. Time has stopped meaning the same thing to it at every moment, which is what aging is.

milestones.title: KPZ growth on circular geometry — interfaces wrapping around a torus, GUE-Tracy-Widom distribution of fluctuations
milestones.result: machine check passed; reviewed 2026-08-02 — Ben's delegated batch approval, substance reviewed by Claude. The lab's first milestone that watches a surface rather than spins. A 1+1d interface was grown on a periodic ring under single-step (corner) growth — the textbook lattice KPZ model, equivalent to TASEP under the usual slope↔particle map — with sublattice-parallel updates that are exact here rather than approximate (same-parity sites are never adjacent, so no two corner flips can interfere; the same checkerboard argument that makes `ising.py`'s red/black sweep exact). Measured on L=4096 over 64 rings and 8,000 sweeps: β = 0.3127 against the exact KPZ 1/3 (R²=0.9994 over 29 points spanning t∈[23, 8000], ~2.5 decades), α = 0.4840 from the saturated width across L=16…192 against the exact 1/2, giving z = α/β = 1.548 vs the exact 3/2 and 1/z = 0.646 vs the exact 2/3 — the milestone's "2/3 in space", derived from the two measured exponents rather than assumed. What makes the 1/3 a measurement rather than a fit: the same width estimator and the same scaling-window rule were pointed at two more growth rules whose exponents are exactly known and different — Edwards–Wilkinson (KPZ minus the (∇h)² term) came out 0.2354 against its exact 1/4, and random deposition 0.5003 against its exact 1/2. Random deposition is the strongest anchor in the milestone because it is not an exponent but a closed form, w²(t) = p(1−p)t at every t with nothing fitted; the run tracks it to 0.6%. A pipeline that manufactured β=1/3 out of any curve would have to report 1/3 three times, and `check_m17` refuses the run unless all three land on their own exact values and genuinely separate. The distribution: height fluctuations came out skewed −0.1651 (droplet/curved) and −0.2732 (flat) against the Tracy–Widom predictions −0.2241 (GUE) and −0.2935 (GOE) — each geometry landing nearer its own law by 2.2× and 2.4×. The negative sign is the prediction, not a bug: the local-minimum density is exactly q(1−q) (brute-forced in the tests), so v(u) = (p/2)(1−u²) and the KPZ nonlinearity λ = ∂²v/∂u² = −p < 0, which predicts the mirrored Tracy–Widom law. Skewness is the graded statistic because it is invariant under the affine rescaling χ=(h−v_∞t)/(Γt)^{1/3}, so neither model constant has to be fitted. Boundary: β sits 0.021 below the exact 1/3 — the documented preasymptotic approach from below, and the tell that this is the finite fit window rather than a defect is that EW misses its own exact 1/4 by 0.015 in the same direction while RD, which has no correlation time to be preasymptotic about, lands essentially exactly. The distributional claim is class assignment, not a full Tracy–Widom collapse: the droplet's third moment is the least-converged graded number in the run (gap 0.059, 1.9× its sampling sigma, against a ±0.06 band), and the report's boundary text is derived from the measured moment gaps rather than hand-written, so prose and data cannot drift apart. Kurtosis is carried as evidence and deliberately not graded. Report reports/2026-07-22-m17.html.
milestones.question_plain: When a surface grows by piling up randomly — like a coffee stain creeping outward or a flame front advancing — do its bumps and wrinkles follow a hidden universal law?
milestones.why_it_matters: A startling range of growing, spreading things share one mathematical fingerprint, and reproducing it would tie the windowsill lab to one of the deepest patterns in non-equilibrium physics.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — the surface roughened as time to the power 0.313 against the predicted 1/3, and to make sure that wasn't the ruler's doing, the same ruler measured two simpler growth rules and each landed on its own different known answer (0.235 vs exact 1/4; 0.500 vs exact 1/2, tracked to 0.6%). Even the lopsidedness of the wrinkles leaned the way the deep theory says it should, for both shapes of growth.

milestones.title: Directed percolation in 2+1d at the absorbing-state transition
milestones.result: machine check passed; promoted 2026-08-14 — Ben delegated approval, substance and claim boundary reviewed by Codex. The lab's first absorbing-state transition: every rung up to M17 relaxed toward an equilibrium the dynamics could always leave again, but here the all-zero lattice is a trap with no thermal escape, and the transition is between activity surviving forever and activity dying. Model: a synchronous probabilistic cellular automaton on a periodic L=2048 lattice, five parents per site (itself + 4 nearest neighbours), each transmitting independently — `P(active) = 1 − (1−p)^n`. All-zero is absorbing by construction: n=0 gives probability exactly 0. The graded claim is a bracket, not a single number, and that is the methodological point. Because `δ_eff(t) = −dln ρ/dln t` is monotonically decreasing in p, a subcritical and a supercritical run bound the true exponent between their curves — a statement a finite lattice can actually support, where quoting δ at one p would demand knowing p_c to more digits than this box resolves and would quietly turn an unresolved p_c into a fitted knob. Result: δ bracketed to [0.4114, 0.5450] over t ∈ [1000, 5000] by a straddling pair at p = 0.22410 / 0.22420 (R² = 0.9978 / 0.9928, 4001 points each), which contains the (2+1)d DP value 0.4505 (Hinrichsen 2000, Adv. Phys. 49, 815, from β = 0.583(4), ν_∥ = 1.295(6)) and excludes the mean-field value 1.0 — the second half matters as much as the first, because without it the run has shown only that something decreases, not whether its decay is consistent with the non-mean-field DP benchmark (d_c = 4, so 2+1d sits genuinely below the upper critical dimension). The straddle is verified, not assumed: curvature of δ_eff over the last two octaves is +1.209 at p_low and −0.153 at p_high, opposite signs, and the runner refuses if they are not. p_c = 0.22415 ± 0.00005 is a measurement — the bracket midpoint and half-width — never read from a table; it is a property of this transmission rule, not a universal number, which is why only δ is compared to the literature. Three controls, each catching a specific lie. Deep subcritical (p=0.15): the decay must be exponential, not a power law, and the two fits are compared head to head — exponential R²=0.9953 beats power-law R²=0.9383, catching the pipeline's likeliest failure of calling any falling curve critical. Deep supercritical (p=0.32): density saturates at ρ=0.736 with δ_eff=0.0008. Absorbing-state integrity: from an all-zero lattice at p=0.9, nothing switches on across 200 steps — a sign slip or off-by-one in the parent count would let activity appear from nothing and every exponent above it would describe a different model. Finite-size guard is headroom, not extrapolation: ξ_⊥ ~ t^(1/z) with z=1.766 reaches 457 sites at t=50000, so L/ξ = 4.5. 227 s on the RX 6900 XT. Independent promotion rerun, 2026-08-14: a second full L=2048/batch=4/t=50000 execution on an RTX 3070 Ti bracketed δ to [0.4172, 0.5592] (R² = 0.9982 / 0.9944), again with opposite curvature signs (+0.836 / −0.253) and all three controls passing in 311 s. Boundary: this shows a decay exponent consistent with the (2+1)d DP benchmark and brackets that exponent and locates p_c to the bracket width; it is not a precision determination of either. One lattice size, so no finite-size-scaling collapse is claimed. A `--quick` CPU pass ships a `[~]` null by design — at L=256/t=2000 the bracket is [0.1691, 0.3552] and misses, which is the convention working. Report `reports/2026-08-07-m18.html`; rerun `lab m18`.
milestones.question_plain: If an activity can either spread to its neighbours or fizzle out for good, is there a knife's-edge setting where it just barely survives forever?
milestones.why_it_matters: This simplest model of epidemics, forest fires, and chain reactions captures the universal tipping point between extinction and survival, a pattern that shows up far beyond physics.
milestones.result_plain: Yes, within the resolution this machine can support. The lab ran just below and just above the knife edge, then kept the answer as the range between them instead of tuning one run until it looked exact. That range contains the published value for this kind of spreading process and rules out the simpler large-system approximation. A second full run on a different GPU landed on the same conclusion. Three controls ran alongside: activity far below the edge died in a clearly different way, activity far above it levelled off, and a completely empty grid never switched itself back on. This is a bounded consistency check, not a precision measurement or proof that every feature of the model belongs to the same family.

milestones.title: Kuramoto synchronization transition, calibrated
milestones.result: K_c = 1.0007 vs exact 2γ = 1.0000, rel. err 0.07%; reviewed and approved by Ben 2026-08-02. The lab's first non-lattice milestone: no sites, no neighbours, no temperature — 2000 oscillators on a circle, coupled only through their own centroid `r·e^{iψ} = ⟨e^{iθ}⟩`, integrated with fixed-step RK4. The pair coupling collapses exactly to the mean-field form `K·r·sin(ψ−θ_i)`, which is what makes an N=2000 sweep an O(N)-per-step NumPy CPU job (≈105 s) rather than a GPU one. Sweeping 25 couplings over [0, 4γ] at γ=0.5, the susceptibility-style fluctuation χ(K) = N·Var_t(r) — the same estimator M04/M05/M06 peak-locate in temperature, refined with the same 3-point parabola — peaks at K_c = 1.0007 against the exact 2γ = 1.0000 (rel. err 0.07%). The stronger claim is not the peak but the curve: above the transition the mean-field solution is a closed form with nothing fitted, `r(K) = √(1 − K_c/K)`, and the measured coherence matches it to 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ across 7 un-fitted couplings — the same role random deposition's exact `w²=p(1−p)t` plays in M17 and the Nishimori-line energy identity plays in M14. A pipeline that manufactured a plausible transition would still have to reproduce seven coherence values it never fitted. The negative control closes the other end: at K=0 the measured ⟨r⟩ = 0.0203 is nothing but the random-walk centroid of N scattered phases, 1/√N = 0.0224 — a collapsed frequency draw (all ω equal) would order at zero coupling and is caught before any peak is fitted. Natural frequencies are drawn by deterministic inverse-CDF quantile sampling on the grid (i+½)/N rather than from a generator, so the set is exactly antisymmetric (Σω = 0, no spurious ψ drift) and carries no sampling noise on top of the finite-size effect being measured; the Lorentzian's tails are clipped at |ω| ≤ 40γ, which — unlike truncating and renormalizing — leaves g(0) and therefore `K_c = 2/(πg(0))` exactly unchanged while keeping |ω|·dt ≪ 2π so no fast drifter is aliased into a spurious near-stationary lock. Boundary: the exact K_c = 2γ is an N → ∞ result and the sweep is a finite grid, so this is a calibrated finite-N estimate, not a precision measurement. Both systematics were measured before the tolerance was declared, not assumed: the estimate approaches 2γ from above — 1.0504 at N=250, 1.0256 at N=500, 1.0083 at N=1000, 1.0007 at N=2000 — and by N=2000 the run-to-run scatter from the initial condition (a second seed gave 0.9910) has overtaken the finite-N shift. The floor under both is the sweep's own resolution ΔK = γ/6 = 0.0833, which is what sets `check_k01`'s ±0.10 band — the grid, not the shipped run's luck. dt = 0.02 was cross-checked against dt = 0.01: the two agree on the graded peak to four decimals, so the number is a property of the model and not the integrator. The steepest-rise cross-check estimator is carried but deliberately not graded — `r(K) = √(1−K_c/K)` has infinite slope at K_c⁺, so a central difference on a finite grid can never place it better than ≈0.8·ΔK high, and it lands at 1.068 at every N and seed tried; that is a known property of the estimator, which is exactly why the fluctuation peak is the headline. Green-leaf review: Ben, 2026-08-02, same day as the machine pass.
milestones.question_plain: If you fill a room with clocks that all tick at slightly different speeds, and let each one nudge the others, how hard do they have to pull before they suddenly all tick together?
milestones.why_it_matters: The same tipping point governs fireflies flashing in unison, heart cells beating as one, and power grids staying in step — and there is an exact answer to check the lab against.
milestones.result_plain: The clocks snapped into step at a nudging strength of 1.0007, against the exact answer of 1. The harder test: above that point, theory predicts the whole curve of how much they agree, and the lab reproduced seven points on it to within two ten-thousandths with nothing fitted. With no nudging at all the clocks read 0.0203 together, which is just the accidental agreement of 2000 random things, so the effect is not an artefact of the setup.

milestones.title: The susceptibility's shape, and whether it survives N
milestones.question_plain: A room of clocks is at its twitchiest somewhere between total disagreement and perfect lockstep — but is the exact spot where that happens a real law, or just a side effect of how many clocks were in the room?
milestones.why_it_matters: An earlier experiment in this lab fitted a tidy formula putting that sweet spot at 40% agreement; if the number is really just counting the crowd, then anyone building on the formula would be quietly wrong at every other size. Checking it also gives the lab a chance to measure a number physicists already published — the honest way to find out whether a windowsill instrument can be trusted.
milestones.result_plain: The twitchiest point does sit somewhere in the middle, at every crowd size from 250 clocks up to 4000. But it is not at 40% agreement, and it slides lower as the crowd grows — so this lab's earlier 40% was measuring the size of the room, not a law, and that claim is withdrawn. Measuring the slide directly: agreement falls as the crowd size to the power 0.401, give or take 0.017, against the 0.39 published for this exact setup in 2015. The two agree well within their error bars.

milestones.title: Daido vs Hong: is the susceptibility exponent asymmetric across K_c?
milestones.question_plain: Right at the edge where a crowd of clocks falls into step, does the crowd react just as sharply coming from below the edge as from above — or is the edge lopsided?
milestones.why_it_matters: Two sets of physicists have published opposite answers to this about the exact system this lab already runs, and nobody has settled it. It is the first question on the page where the lab is not checking a known answer but trying to break a tie.

milestones.title: Pulse-coupled fireflies: measure the Mirollo–Strogatz almost-sure synchronization theorem.
milestones.question_plain: If a swarm of identical fireflies each flashes on its own clock, and every flash gives all the others a tiny push toward flashing, must the whole swarm always end up flashing in perfect unison?
milestones.why_it_matters: In 1990 two mathematicians proved the answer is yes — always, from almost any start. Real riverbank fireflies in Southeast Asia actually do this. A proved theorem is the sternest test the lab can face: there is no error bar to hide in, every single trial has to make it.

milestones.title: Calibrate the number stack
milestones.result: machine check passed; reviewed 2026-08-02 — Ben's delegated batch approval, substance reviewed by Claude. The runner generated the first 40 Fibonacci entries locally and matched their exact UTF-8 bytes against the official OEIS A000045 b-file prefix, then independently ran Lucas–Lehmer for M31=2^31−1 and reached final residue 0. The receipt pins the retrieved 429,385-byte OEIS source by SHA-256 and retains the exact compared prefix; `check_c01` regenerates the bytes and reruns Lucas–Lehmer rather than trusting cached pass fields. milestones.question_plain: Before we hunt for new numbers, can we prove our machine even does math we can trust?
milestones.why_it_matters: Every later number-hunting result is worthless unless the basic arithmetic is provably correct first.
milestones.result_plain: A check of the arithmetic itself, not a finding. The machine rebuilt the first 40 Fibonacci numbers and matched the official catalogue byte for byte, then re-ran a known primality test on 2 to the 31st minus 1 and got the expected remainder of zero. This exists so the number-handling can be trusted before it is pointed at anything unknown.

milestones.why_it_matters: It puts a windowsill machine into a real global hunt where home volunteers have actually discovered record-breaking primes.

milestones.question_plain: Can we add new, checked terms to a famous catalog of number sequences and have them officially accepted?
milestones.why_it_matters: It turns idle computing time into a permanent, credited addition to a reference mathematicians actually use.

milestones.title: Calibrate photometry
milestones.result: machine check passed; reviewed 2026-08-02 — Ben's delegated batch approval, substance reviewed by Claude. Eight official mission-produced TESS SPOC light curves for confirmed WASP-18 b / TIC 100100827 were downloaded from MAST and SHA-256 pinned. A dependency-free FITS reader selected quality-zero PDCSAP cadences; a blind Sector-2 transit search seeded an ephemeris, then the multi-year baseline across Sectors 2,3,29,30,69,96,103,104 refined 177 accepted transit timings without using the catalog value in the fit. Regrading those timings gives P=0.94145236 d vs NASA Exoplanet Archive 0.94145223±0.00000024 d (Δ=0.00000013 d); the median local transit depth is 1.022% vs 1.041±0.022% (Δ=0.019%). Both fall inside the published error bars. `check_a01` refits the saved timings and depth samples. Boundary: calibration on public archive photometry, not a new planet detection, independent observation, or ExoFOP submission; raw FITS bytes remain at MAST and are pinned by URI/size/hash.
milestones.question_plain: From free telescope data, can we catch a known planet dimming its star and measure its year correctly?
milestones.why_it_matters: It proves our analysis of real survey data lands inside the numbers professional astronomers already published.
milestones.result_plain: From eight public telescope visits spanning seven years, the lab timed 177 crossings and measured the planet's year at 0.94145236 days, against the published 0.94145223. That is a difference of about 11 milliseconds. The star dims by 1.022% as the planet passes, against a published 1.041%. Both sit inside the published error bars. The catalogue value was never used in the fit.

milestones.title: Recover a known variable star's light curve and period; register an AAVSO observer code and submit one validated observation
milestones.result: recovery half measured 2026-08-23, machine gate PASSED, awaiting human review; the AAVSO half is untouched and stays open — registering an observer code and submitting a validated observation is an account action a human takes, and no part of it is claimed here. Six known variables across four pulsator classes, recovered blind: 6/6 inside their own resolution element, 6/6 clear of control. The sample is declared as NAMES, not TIC ids, because a TIC id is already an answer to "which star is this?" — the question A05 got wrong on TIC 77044472 — so coordinate resolution is inside what gets graded, and a cone holding two TICs refuses rather than taking the first row. Periods come from the dominant frequency of a least-squares amplitude spectrum over a band fixed before any spectrum was computed (0.05-120 c/d), refined below the grid by parabolic interpolation; the catalogued period is read only at grading time, from AAVSO VSX — the milestone's own venue — cached and SHA-256 pinned so `check_a02` re-derives every number offline from the photometry and never from the receipt. The bar is derived, not chosen: one Rayleigh element, dP = P^2/T, the smallest period difference the baseline can distinguish; the tightest margin still beats it 16x and the widest by ~1e4. Measured: AI Vel 0.1115740 d vs 0.111574 (rel 5.0e-08), SX Phe 4.8e-06, AE UMa 5.7e-06, XX Cyg 9.5e-06, beta Cep 5.0e-05, RR Lyr 7.4e-04. The ordering was predicted before the run: RR Lyr is Blazhko-modulated (VSX type RRAB/BL), so a single 27-day sector measures that sector's period and not the published mean — the module says so in a comment written before any star was fetched, and its residual came back the largest of the six by more than an order of magnitude over the next worst. Every target also carries a control: the same flux shuffled against the same timestamps, which keeps the noise and destroys the coherence; the real peaks stand 19-29x above it. Boundary: six bright, well-studied stars whose periods are decades old, so this is a calibration of the instrument against the catalogue, not a new period for anything; amplitudes are reported and never graded, since PDCSAP's corrections are tuned for transits and only approximately right for a high-amplitude pulsator; delta Cep and DY Peg were declared and skipped with a named reason — no SPOC two-minute photometry. Receipt `reports/receipts/run-2026-08-23-1425-a02.json` (the dated render `reports/2026-08-23-a02.html` is gitignored like every other per-run render); rerun `lab a02`.
milestones.question_plain: Can we follow a star that brightens and dims, time its rhythm, and add a real observation to the amateur record?
milestones.why_it_matters: Some stars pulse like a heartbeat, swelling and shrinking on a rhythm you could set a clock by. Timing one is how you prove a telescope pipeline actually works, because the right answer is already written down by other people — so there is nowhere to hide.
milestones.result_plain: Six stars, given to the lab as names and nothing else. It found each one in the public telescope archive, watched it brighten and dim, and worked out its rhythm without ever being told the answer — then checked all six against the catalogue afterwards. All six right. The best was a star called AI Vel, whose pulse the lab timed to within about five thousandths of a second per day. The hardest was RR Lyrae, and we said before starting that it would be: its rhythm slowly wanders, so a month of watching can only ever catch that month's version of it. It came last, exactly as predicted. The other half of this experiment is still open — sending an observation to the amateur astronomers' database is something a person has to do, not a program.

milestones.title: Reprocess one open LIGO/Virgo event from GWOSC and reproduce its published chirp mass within error
milestones.result: a controlled null: the pipeline is validated to 24× the required precision and the event is still not recovered. Matched filtering against 3.5PN TaylorF2 stationary-phase inspiral templates, written on numpy alone — no scipy, no h5py, no gwpy — in the same dependency-free spirit as A01's FITS reader. The target choice is a physics argument, and it is the first result. An inspiral-only template is the right model only while the binary is inspiralling in band: for GW150914's ~66 M☉ system `f_ISCO = 1/(6^1.5 π M)` is 67 Hz, so the inspiral occupies only 35–67 Hz and essentially all the SNR sits in a merger-ringdown TaylorF2 does not describe — which is why LIGO used full IMR waveforms for it. Measured directly: releasing the ISCO truncation on GW150914 moved the estimate from 24.8 to 31.7 M☉ source-frame in H1 and to 35.8 in L1 — a 4 M☉ inter-detector disagreement against a ±1.7 published bar, i.e. the estimator advertising its own unreliability. So A03 targets GW170817, a binary neutron star that spends ~3583 GW cycles above 25 Hz, where the model is correct. The positive control passes decisively. A software injection at the published detector-frame chirp mass (1.19786 M☉) is recovered at 1.19782 in H1 (error 4.0×10⁻⁵) and 1.19784 in L1 (error 2.0×10⁻⁵), SNR 38.1 / 37.8, merger time to 0.1 ms — 24× tighter than the published ±0.001. The sky is not. The event itself returns SNR 6.6 against a 10.6 / 10.8 background in both detectors: no detection, and the argmax chirp masses (1.141, 1.146 source-frame) neither agree with each other nor with 1.186. Two ancillary findings landed blind and are real: the GW170817 Livingston glitch was found without being looked for, at 209σ, −1.06 s from merger, and gated; and on GW150914 the event is the loudest 10 ms envelope in 24 s — 19.1σ in H1, 15.7σ in L1 — with the two detectors agreeing on merger time to 7 ms, inside the 10 ms Hanford–Livingston light-travel limit. Whitening was validated before anything was claimed (in-band unit variance 0.987/0.998, kurtosis 3.0 in clean H1). Four prototypes were discarded on the way, and one of them matters: an early filter reported chirp masses of 1.174 and 1.238 that were pure noise — proven by an injection test the pipeline could not see, which is exactly why the control is now permanent and `check_a03` refuses to grade the sky at all when the control fails. Boundary — the honest reason this is amber, not green: the injection is drawn from the same 3.5PN TaylorF2 family as the search template, so it validates the filter, whitening, gating and grid, and deliberately does not validate the waveform's fidelity to a real source. A real BNS carries spin, tidal and higher-order structure this template omits, and that model mismatch — together with a single fixed η=0.2490 and a background max of ~10.7 that real searches suppress with χ² signal-consistency vetoes — is the leading candidate for the gap. Reproducing the published value needs the waveform physics, not more compute. Report `reports/2026-08-07-a03.html`; rerun `lab a03`.
milestones.question_plain: From open gravitational-wave data, can we re-measure the mass of a collision that shook spacetime and match the official answer?
milestones.why_it_matters: It shows a home machine can independently re-derive a landmark physics result from the same public data the discoverers used.
milestones.result_plain: No. And the interesting part is how carefully it failed. The lab first fed its own pipeline a fake collision planted in the real detector data, and the pipeline found it and weighed it about twenty-four times more precisely than the published error bar — so the control passed. Pointed at the real 2017 neutron-star collision, it found nothing strong enough to call a detection, and said so rather than fitting the answer it already knew. On the way past it did find something real it was not looking for: a known instrumental glitch in the Livingston detector at 209 sigma, 1.06 seconds before the collision. Reproducing the published mass needs better wave physics, not more computer time.

milestones.title: Blind transit search of a deterministic sample from one TESS sector; vet the candidates and report a recovered planet
milestones.result: machine check passed; promoted 2026-08-14 — Ben delegated approval, substance and claim boundary reviewed by Codex. A01 recovered a planet the pipeline was TOLD about, searching a narrow window around WASP-18 b's known period; A04 removes that — the search gets light curves with no labels, no periods and no hint which host anything. Three of A01's assumptions had to go: the grid widened from 0.85–1.05 d to 0.5–15 d; the curve is detrended by a running median (stellar variability swamps a 1% transit); and ranking moved from raw box depth — useless across stars, since a noisy one wins while hosting nothing — to SDE, which is self-normalising and therefore comparable. Result: both designated planets recovered blind and ranked 1st and 2nd — HIP 65 A b at P=0.98124 d vs published 0.98097 (SDE 14.2) and WASP-18 b at 0.94164 vs 0.94145 (SDE 10.2), catalog periods read only at grading time and never entering the search. The threshold is measured, not chosen: injections at 1.0/0.4/0.2% depth all recovered (SDE 8.8/9.2/10.1) and the noise floor over 22 sub-threshold targets tops out at 6.6, so SDE ≥ 8 sits in a real gap; `check_a04` refuses if that gap closes. The vetting step earned its keep twice. TIC 211438925 was flagged blind at P=4.9014 d, survived odd-even and secondary-eclipse tests as a `planet-candidate`, and the report-time catalog cross-check identified it as WASP-20 b (TOI 194.01, disposition KP, published 4.89962 d) — a third known planet recovered without being designated, and an independent validation of the vetting itself. TIC 339607421 (4.78% depth, 11 events) was flagged and correctly rejected as an eclipsing binary by an odd-even depth alternation; an earlier run's TIC 287328866, in no TOI or confirmed-planet table, separated at 11σ the same way. Five defects were found and fixed, all in the layer that decides what a detection MEANS — the search itself was right on the first attempt and never wrong since: the 'deterministic sample' was seeded from a hash of the whole pool, so consecutive runs shared almost no targets (now consistent hashing, stable under pool change); the page-capped listing was reported as 'the sector'; the grid reached to 15 d on a 27-day baseline, returning P=14.86 d at SDE 10.1 with under two transits and no possible odd-even test (now capped at baseline/3); `planet-candidate` was granted on ~1e-5 depths with the odd-epoch depth negative (now both parities must show a real positive dip at ≥5σ); and `planet-candidate` was granted at P=0.5000 d, exactly the search floor — a railing artifact that would have entered a public report (now grid-railed periods are rejected at both edges before any other test). Each is a test named for the target that produced it. Boundary: a deterministic SAMPLE of one sector, not the sector — a real TESS sector holds thousands of 2-minute targets — so no completeness or occurrence-rate statement is implied. milestones.question_plain: Can a blind search of a small, predeclared sample from one telescope survey recover real planets without being told where to look?
milestones.why_it_matters: It tests whether the search and vetting can find real signals without leaking the catalogue answer into the hunt — the calibration needed before any genuinely new candidate could be trusted.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — three times, with the labels taken away. The earlier planet-weighing run was told where to look; this one searched 26 stars with no planet names or periods. The two planets it was graded on came back first and second in its own ranking. It also flagged a third star nobody had asked about, put it through the same checks, and only afterwards identified it as another already-known planet. During the debugging runs it rejected deep, convincing signals that were alternating eclipses or artifacts at the edge of the search range. The cutoff was measured rather than chosen: fake transits at three depths all cleared it, while twenty-two quieter stars stayed below it. The claim is narrow: a blind sample recovered known planets and measured its own noise floor. It is not a discovery, a survey of the whole sector, or a submission for follow-up.

milestones.title: Survey-grade detection statistics: can every threshold-crossing event carry its own measured false-alarm probability?
milestones.question_plain: When the planet-hunt flags a dip in a star's light, can the lab measure — for that exact star — how often pure chance would fake a dip just as convincing, and how small a dip that star could even show?
milestones.why_it_matters: A hunt that cannot price its own false alarms will eventually announce noise. In one day of pilot runs a signal held 'planet candidate' for forty minutes before being unmasked as a pulsing star, and another matched a catalog entry the community had already refuted — so every flagged signal needs its own measured odds, and the machine's strongest verdict stays 'a lead awaiting human review', never 'a planet'.

milestones.question_plain: With the statistics proven, can the same search run on a newer patch of sky — one the community has had less time to comb — with every test for killing a false signal committed in advance?
milestones.why_it_matters: Declaring the refutation tests before touching the data is what keeps an exciting blip from bending the rules that judge it.

milestones.question_plain: If you watch Jupiter's four big moons for four months, do they keep the exact mathematical rhythm Kepler and Laplace wrote down centuries ago?
milestones.why_it_matters: Three of the moons are locked in a gravitational waltz so precise it has held for billions of years — recovering it from public ephemerides proves this lab can measure celestial clockwork end to end.
milestones.result_plain: Yes — all four moons land on Kepler's line, Jupiter's mass falls out of the fit, and Io, Europa and Ganymede keep the Laplace rhythm while Callisto, the outsider, proves the rhythm is real by breaking it.

milestones.why_it_matters: Genuinely unguessable numbers are the bedrock of secure communication, and a published feed lets anyone use and check them.

milestones.title: Fold HP lattice sequences blind and recover ground states proven in-house.
milestones.result: machine gate PASSED, awaiting human review.
milestones.question_plain: A protein is a chain of beads that folds itself into one particular shape, and the shape is what it does for a living. If you strip that down to its simplest honest version — beads that either love water or don't, folded on graph paper — can a computer find the single best fold out of the millions available?
milestones.why_it_matters: Finding the best fold is one of those problems that gets impossibly harder as the chain gets longer, which is why it has been the standard test for folding software for thirty years. The trap is that a search can always report SOME fold and call it the best one. So for short chains this lab checks every single possible fold first, one by one, until the true answer is proven rather than believed — and only then lets the search loose, knowing nothing, to see if it finds the same thing.
milestones.result_plain: Seven chains, seven times the search found exactly the fold that the exhaustive check had already proven was the best one. There is also a control that needs no computer at all: on graph paper, some chains are built so their water-hating beads can never touch each other, no matter how you fold them — so the answer has to be zero, and both the exhaustive check and the search say zero. What this does not do is fold a real protein: this is the simple version, on flat graph paper, and nothing here describes the shape of anything alive.
